questions.prompt: Which cost usually dominates a software system's lifetime?

options.text: The cost of writing the first version
The cost of change — modifying the system over time
The cost of the programming language license
The cost of naming the project

questions.explanation: Most of a system's cost is paid after it first works, in the repeated cost of change. Good architecture exists to keep that cost low.

questions.prompt: In Martin's framing, structure/architecture is best described as:

options.text: Important but rarely urgent — so it's easy to neglect

questions.explanation: Behavior feels urgent; structure is important but rarely urgent, so teams that always chase the urgent let structure decay.

questions.prompt: Software is called 'soft' because, unlike hardware, it is meant to be easy to ______.
questions.explanation: The word 'software' contrasts with 'hardware': software should be easy to change, and architecture keeps it that way.

questions.prompt: Which are genuine benefits of investing in architecture? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keeping options open by deferring decisions
Making each change cheaper and more localized
Guaranteeing the first version ships fastest
Reducing the risk of each change

questions.explanation: Architecture lowers the cost and risk of change and keeps options open. It does NOT guarantee the fastest first version — that often costs a bit more up front.

questions.prompt: Order these tasks from how urgent stakeholders typically feel them (most urgent first) — the trap that lets structure rot.
questions.explanation: Behavior (bugs, features) feels most urgent; structural work feels least urgent — which is exactly why it gets neglected even though it's important.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: What the software does right now
How cheaply the behavior can be changed
The ability to defer or reverse a decision cheaply
Paying architecture's cost with no payoff

questions.explanation: Behavior is present value; structure governs the cost of change; optionality is deferring decisions; over-engineering is architecture without benefit.
